text: Given two strings s and t, return true if t is an anagram of s. There's a follow-up: what if the inputs contain Unicode characters?

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — an anagram means t uses exactly the same characters as s, each the same number of times, just reordered. So it's really: do the two strings have identical character counts? And are there any constraints on the input — which characters can appear?
Exactly. For the base problem, assume lowercase English letters.
Got it. Let me run through examples. Anagram and nagaram is true — same letters, same counts. Rat and car is false — t has a c that s doesn't.

Let me think. A naive approach would sort both strings and compare them — that's n log n. This problem reminds me of a frequency-count pattern: order doesn't matter, only counts do, and counting is linear. I'll build a count table from s by incrementing, then walk t decrementing. If any character goes negative, or t has a character s never had, it's not an anagram. And there's a free early check: if the lengths differ, return false immediately.
Why does goes negative mean it's not an anagram?

Frequency of c is the inventory of c's that s supplied and t can still consume. Each c in t spends one. If t tries to spend a c when the inventory is already zero, dropping to minus one means t has more c's than s — the counts don't match.

Here's the plan. One: if the lengths differ, return false. Two: walk s and add one to each character's count — that's the inventory. Three: walk t and spend one per character; if the key is missing or the count drops below zero, return false. Otherwise return true. One thing worth flagging — I'll write the guard as count of c equals zero, or minus-minus freq of c below zero, so the count check short-circuits. Otherwise, indexing a missing key would silently insert it. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The length guard comes first. Then an unordered map from char to int: one loop over s builds the counts, and one loop over t spends them, returning false the moment a key is missing or a count goes negative. If t survives, return true. The easy line to get wrong is that guard: count must be checked before the decrement, and the or short-circuits, so I never create a key by accident. That's linear time, and order k space, where k is the number of distinct characters.
You didn't check that all counts are zero at the end. Isn't that a bug?

It's safe because of the length guard. The increments total the size of s, and the decrements total the size of t; those are equal. So if nothing ever went negative, every decrement legally came out of a positive inventory, and the total removed equals the total added. That forces every count back to exactly zero. Nothing went negative is equivalent to all zero. Without the length check that equivalence breaks — s equals a b, t equals a, would leave the b unchecked and falsely return true. That's exactly why the length guard comes first.

Let's dry-run the two failure modes. Rat versus car, expected false: s builds one r, one a, one t. The row that matters is t's first character, c — its count is zero, so I return false. That's the character s never had. Aabb versus abbb, expected false: the row that matters is the fourth character, b, which drives the count of b from zero to minus one, so I return false. That's the overspent case. And anagram versus nagaram never trips either check, so it returns true. All three match.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear, space is order k. And this answers the follow-up directly. Because I used an unordered map rather than a fixed array of twenty-six, the idea carries straight over to Unicode: any character, keyed by its full code point, can be a key, and the space grows with the distinct characters actually present. If I'd hardcoded c minus a into a twenty-six slot array — which is faster for guaranteed lowercase — a Unicode character would index out of bounds. So the rule is: bounded, small alphabet, use an array; large or unknown, use a hash map.

Strong. You reduced anagram to a count comparison, explained the negative-inventory logic and why the length guard lets you skip the all-zero check, and the map choice answered the Unicode follow-up. Nice.
